parts.intro: You will hear a man phoning the secretary of a community choir to ask about joining.

turns.text: Good evening, Riverside Community Choir, this is Martha speaking.
Oh, hi. My name's Callum. I saw a poster in the post office saying you're looking for new singers, and I wondered if I could get a bit more information.
Of course. We're always happy to hear from new people, especially men, to be honest. We're a bit short of tenors and basses at the moment. Have you sung in a choir before?
Only at school, and that was a long time ago. I sing in the car a lot, though.

Well, that's how most of us started. So, let me tell you how it works. We rehearse once a week. The poster probably says Tuesday, because that's what it was last year, but we've moved to Wednesday now, as the room wasn't available on Tuesdays any more.
Wednesday is actually better for me. What time do you start?
We used to begin at half past seven, but people said they got home too late, so now we start at 7:15 and finish at a quarter past nine, with a short break in the middle for tea.
That sounds fine. And where are the rehearsals? Is it the church on Mill Street?

No, we left the church a couple of years ago because it was so cold in winter. We meet at Hartfield Primary School now. Normally we'd use the main hall, but it's being repainted this term, so for the moment we're in the library, which is on the first floor. There's a lift if anyone needs it.
Great. Now, I imagine there's some kind of membership fee?
There is. The full annual fee is £95, but for anyone joining for the first time it's reduced, so you'd pay £85 for your first year. That covers the hire of the room and the music, which we lend you.
So I don't need to buy any scores?

No, we provide all the music. You just need to bring a pencil to every rehearsal, because the director is always asking us to mark things on the music, like where to breathe. Please don't use a pen, though, because the scores have to be returned at the end of the season.
Got it. Do I have to do an audition?
Not really. You'll just have a short chat with our musical director, so he can find out whether you're a tenor or a bass. His name is Daniel Ferrow.
Is that F-A-R-R-O-W?
Nearly. It's Ferrow, F-E-R-R-O-W. He's lovely, and very patient with beginners.
And what about performances? How many concerts do you give?

Three main events a year. The first is our winter concert. For years we held it in the town hall, but this year we've been invited to sing at the museum, in the big gallery with the old steam engines. The sound in there is wonderful.
When is that?
It was going to be on the seventh of December, but that clashed with the Christmas market, so it'll be on the fourteenth instead. It starts at seven.
And after that?
In the spring we do something a bit different. We sing outdoors at the harbour, on the first weekend of May, as part of the town's boat festival. It's free for the public, and people bring picnics.
That sounds fun. Is there anything special I need to wear for the concerts?

For the winter concert everyone wears black, which most people have already. But for the summer concert in July we all wear white shirts, so you might need to buy one. The ladies wear a coloured scarf as well, but you don't need to worry about that.
Fine. I've got a white shirt somewhere. So, can I just turn up next Wednesday?
Yes, please do. Come about ten minutes early so I can give you your music folder. Can I take a phone number, just in case a rehearsal is cancelled?
Lovely. We'll see you on Wednesday, Callum.

parts.intro: You will hear a local radio reporter talking about a new bus route in the town of Ashby.

turns.text: Good morning, and welcome to Ashby Today. Now, if you live on the east side of town, you'll know that getting to the hospital or the college by bus has meant changing at the central station, which can easily add half an hour to your journey. Well, from next month that changes, because the council is launching a brand-new service, the Number 9, which will link the east side directly with the west of town.

The idea for the route didn't actually come from the council or the bus company. It came from a survey organised by students at the college, who asked more than two thousand residents about their travel. What stood out was not that people wanted cheaper fares, or more buses at night, but that they wanted to cross town without changing. The council took the findings seriously, and here we are.

Buses will run every twelve minutes during the day. Some people had hoped for every ten minutes, but the company says it simply doesn't have enough drivers yet. After eight in the evening the service drops to every twenty minutes, and the last bus leaves at about half past eleven.

All the buses on the route will be electric. Now, you might expect the main benefit of that to be cleaner air, and of course that's part of it, but what the drivers I spoke to were most excited about was how quiet the vehicles are. As one of them put it, for the first time in twenty years, he can actually hear what passengers are saying to him.

As for fares, there's no special price for the Number 9. Ordinary tickets and passes will all be accepted. However, for the first two weeks, anyone who travels on the new route can enter a free prize draw for a year's travel pass. You'll find the entry form on the back of the timetable, not online as some people had expected, because the company wants to encourage people to pick up a copy.

And one more thing: the route has been designed with wheelchair users in mind. Every stop on the line has a raised kerb, so the ramp isn't needed, and the buses have space for two wheelchairs rather than the usual one.
So, let me take you through some of the stops on the new route, starting in the east.

The first stop is Kingsmead Park. Many people have asked whether there will be parking there for people who want to leave their car and take the bus into town, and I'm pleased to say there will. A free car park with eighty spaces is being built next to the stop.

Next is Ashby Market. The market is very busy on Saturdays, and to avoid delays the bus won't go into the square itself. Instead, the stop has been moved round the corner to Bridge Street, so please note that change.

Then we come to the Leisure Centre. People going for a swim or to the gym will be glad to hear that this stop will have a proper shelter with heating, which is the first of its kind in Ashby, and it's being tested here before the council decides whether to put them elsewhere.

After that there's the College. Students told the survey team that the existing timetable didn't match their lecture times, so the morning buses on the new route have been timed to arrive ten minutes before classes start. That's something the college has been asking for for years.

And finally, at the western end, there's the Hospital. Here the stop is right at the main entrance, and there's a screen inside the reception area that shows exactly when the next bus is coming, so patients don't have to wait outside in bad weather. A similar screen was planned for the market stop, but it won't be ready until next year.
The full timetable is available from the library and the central station from Friday. Now, let's move on to the weather.

parts.intro: You will hear two business students, Josh and Megan, discussing their case study report with their tutor, Dr Hale.

turns.text: Come in, both of you. So, I've read your case study on the bakery chain, Crumb and Co. Before I give you my comments, how did you feel the project went?
Mostly well, I think. The hardest part was choosing the company. We started with a sportswear firm, but there was almost nothing published about it, so we switched.
And Crumb and Co. had that big expansion and then closed a third of its shops, so we thought there'd be a clear story to analyse.

It certainly is a clear story. Now, overall, I was impressed. What really stood out for me wasn't the research, though that was solid. It was the way you linked the theory from the lectures to what actually happened. A lot of groups just describe events, and then tack a theory on at the end. You used the models to explain the decisions.
That's good to hear. We were worried the theory section was too long.
It's slightly long, but it earns its place. Now, let's talk about the interviews. You spoke to two former store managers. How did you find them?
Through a professional networking site. We sent messages to about fifteen people and two said yes.

That's a reasonable response rate, actually. My concern is different. Both managers had left the company on bad terms, hadn't they? So their views of head office are likely to be rather negative. I'm not saying ignore them, but you need to acknowledge that in the report.
We did think about that. Maybe we could add a sentence in the methods section?
Yes, a short paragraph on the limitations would do it. Now, your financial analysis. You calculated the profit margins for each year, which is fine, but the figures for 2021 look odd.
Oh, that's because the company changed the end of its financial year, so that year was only nine months long.
Right, and that's exactly the kind of thing a reader needs to be told. At the moment it looks like a dramatic fall in sales, when it's really just a shorter year. Put a note under the table.
Okay, we'll do that. What about the conclusion? We weren't sure whether to make recommendations.

The brief doesn't require them, but I'd encourage it. You clearly have views about what the company should have done differently, and recommendations would show you can apply your analysis. Keep them realistic, though. Two or three is plenty.
So, let's think about why the expansion failed. In your view, what were the main causes?
Well, there are a lot of theories online. Some people blame rising flour prices, but every bakery faced those, and the independent bakeries mostly survived.

Right. We think the first real problem was location. They opened new shops in out-of-town retail parks, where people drive in, shop, and leave. Nobody buys a fresh pastry on the way to a furniture store.
That's convincing, and your footfall data supports it.

And the second was staff training. Because they opened so many shops at once, new staff were given one day of training instead of the usual two weeks, and the customer reviews show service got much worse.
People also say the brand was damaged by the new logo, but honestly we couldn't find any evidence that customers cared.

Good. It's important to reject explanations when the evidence doesn't support them. Now, some quick comments on the individual sections of the report. The introduction is fine, but it's very general. The first paragraph could be about any company. Start with Crumb and Co. itself.
Okay. And the literature review?
That's the strongest part. Honestly, I wouldn't change a thing. The methods section is too brief, though. You need to explain how you selected your data, not just list what you used.
And the discussion?
The ideas are good, but the order is confusing. You jump from staffing to location and back again. Group the points by cause and it'll read much more clearly.
Right. And the appendix? We weren't sure it was needed.
It is, but it's got far too much in it. You've included every customer review you found. Choose ten typical ones and refer to them. A reader shouldn't have to wade through two hundred.
That makes sense. Thanks, Dr Hale, this is really helpful.

parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture in a physical geography course about how deserts form.

turns.text: Good afternoon. Today we're looking at deserts, and in particular at the question of why they form where they do. Let's start with a definition, because it's not as obvious as it seems. Most people think of deserts as hot and sandy, but geographers define a desert by its lack of moisture, not by its temperature. The usual threshold is less than about 250 millimetres of precipitation a year, although what really matters is that more water could evaporate than actually falls. By that definition, the largest desert on Earth is not the Sahara, but Antarctica.
So what causes this dryness? There are four main mechanisms, and many deserts are the result of more than one of them.

The first, and by far the most important, is the global circulation of the atmosphere. Near the equator, intense heating makes air rise. As it rises, it cools, and its moisture falls as heavy rain, which is why we find rainforests there. The air, now dry, then spreads towards the poles and sinks at around thirty degrees north and south of the equator. Sinking air warms up and becomes even drier, so clouds rarely form. This band of high pressure explains the location of the Sahara, the Arabian Desert and the deserts of Australia. Geographers call these subtropical deserts. If you look at a world map, you'll notice how neatly many of the great hot deserts line up along these two latitudes, which is one of the clearest examples we have of climate controlling landscape.

The second mechanism involves mountains. When moist air from the ocean meets a mountain range, it is forced upwards, and it drops its rain on the windward slopes. By the time it crosses the summit and descends the other side, it has lost most of its moisture. The dry area on the far side is known as a rain shadow. Several deserts in western North America formed in exactly this way.

Third, there's simple distance from the sea. Air picks up moisture over oceans, and as it travels across a large continent, it gradually rains out. The interior of Asia, thousands of kilometres from any coast, is extremely dry for this reason. The Gobi is the classic example. These are sometimes called continental deserts, and because there's no ocean nearby to moderate temperatures, they have bitterly cold winters as well as hot summers.

The fourth mechanism is less intuitive. Along some western coastlines, cold currents flow from the polar regions towards the equator. The cold water chills the air above it, and cool air holds little moisture. What you get instead of rain is fog. In the coastal deserts of Chile and southern Africa, fog may be the only regular source of water for months, and some plants and insects have evolved to collect it directly. In parts of the Atacama, local communities even use large nets to harvest fog for drinking water.

Now, once a desert exists, what does its surface look like? Again, the popular image misleads us. Sand seas, or ergs, cover only about a fifth of the world's deserts. Much more common are rocky plateaus and plains covered in loose stones, sometimes called desert pavement. These stones are left behind when the wind removes the finer particles around them, a process known as deflation.

And although rain is rare, water is still the main force shaping many desert landscapes. When storms do occur, the ground is often too hard to absorb the water, and there's little vegetation to slow it down, so sudden floods carve deep channels. These dry riverbeds are a common feature, and they can fill within minutes, which makes them genuinely dangerous for travellers. In fact, more people in deserts are thought to drown than to die of thirst, which surprises most students when they first hear it. The channels are known by different local names in different regions, but the process that creates them is the same everywhere.

Finally, I want to mention desertification, which is not the same as the natural formation of deserts. Desertification refers to land in dry regions losing its productivity, usually because of human activity. Overgrazing by livestock is one of the major causes: when animals remove the plant cover, the soil is exposed and blown away. Poor irrigation can also cause damage, because as water evaporates from fields it leaves salt behind, and eventually crops can no longer grow. Next week we'll look at some of the projects trying to reverse this process, including the planting of tree belts along the southern edge of the Sahara.

texts.title: Keeping the same time: the history of standard time zones

paragraphs.text: For most of human history, time was a strictly local matter. Every town set its clocks by the position of the sun, so that noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the local sky. Because the Earth rotates from west to east, this meant that a town only a short distance to the west of its neighbour would keep a slightly earlier time. In an age when travel by horse or on foot was slow, these small discrepancies caused almost no inconvenience. A traveller who arrived in a new town simply adjusted his watch, if he possessed one, to the clock on the church tower or the town hall.

The arrival of the railways in the nineteenth century transformed this situation. Trains covered in hours distances that had previously taken days, and they required timetables that passengers in different towns could understand. Initially, each railway company operated according to the local time of its headquarters, and stations along a line might display two clocks: one showing local time and another showing the company's time. Passengers frequently missed connections, and, more seriously, the confusion contributed to the risk of collisions on single-track lines, where the safe operation of trains depended on precise coordination.

Britain, a comparatively small country with a rapidly expanding network, was among the first to adopt a uniform solution. During the 1840s, railway companies progressively adopted the time kept at the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, which became known as 'railway time'. The electric telegraph made this practical, since time signals could be transmitted from the observatory to stations across the country almost instantaneously. Many towns soon abandoned their local time altogether, although some resisted for years, and legal recognition of a single national time did not arrive until several decades later.

In larger countries, a single national time was impractical. The continental United States spans roughly four hours of solar time, and imposing one time across it would have meant that noon in some regions occurred in what was effectively early morning or late afternoon. By the early 1880s, American railways were using dozens of different local times, and the system had become almost unworkable. In 1883 the railway companies, acting without any government legislation, introduced a system of time zones, each one hour apart. On the day of the changeover, clocks in many cities were adjusted by several minutes, and newspapers described it as 'the day of two noons'.

The railway companies' initiative raised an obvious question: from what point should the world's time zones be measured? In 1884 an international conference was held in Washington to resolve this. Delegates from more than twenty countries voted to adopt the meridian passing through Greenwich as the prime meridian, the line of zero longitude from which all others would be calculated. The choice was largely pragmatic. A majority of the world's shipping already used charts based on Greenwich, so the decision formalised existing practice rather than imposing something new. Not every nation was satisfied, however; France abstained from the vote and continued to use the Paris meridian for its own purposes for several more decades.

Even after the conference, the adoption of standard time zones around the world was gradual and uneven. Some countries chose offsets of half an hour or even a quarter of an hour from Greenwich, reflecting their geographical position or political preferences. Others, particularly large nations governed from a single capital, decided to apply one time zone across territories that might naturally span several. In such places, the sun may rise at a conventional hour in the capital but considerably later in distant regions, a compromise accepted for the sake of administrative simplicity.

Time zones have also proved surprisingly political. Governments have shifted their clocks to align more closely with important trading partners, to signal independence from former rulers, or to make better use of daylight. The introduction of daylight saving time, in which clocks are moved forward during the summer months, added another layer of complexity. Its supporters argued that it reduced the consumption of fuel for lighting, while its critics claimed that the twice-yearly change disrupted sleep and caused confusion. Research on its effects continues to produce mixed results, and a number of countries that once used daylight saving time have since abandoned it.

Today, the global system is coordinated using atomic clocks, which measure time with an accuracy far beyond the capacity of any astronomical observation. Coordinated Universal Time, the modern successor to Greenwich Mean Time, is calculated from the readings of hundreds of such clocks located in laboratories around the world. Yet the underlying logic remains that of the railway age: people in different places agree to share an artificial time, accepting a small departure from the sun in exchange for the enormous benefits of coordination.

texts.title: Seeing with sound: how bats navigate in darkness

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the late eighteenth century, naturalists conducted a series of curious experiments on bats. They found that blindfolded bats could fly through rooms strung with fine wires without touching them, whereas bats whose ears had been blocked collided repeatedly with obstacles. The conclusion that bats somehow 'saw' with their ears was widely ridiculed at the time, largely because nobody could detect any sound coming from the animals. The explanation had to wait until the twentieth century, when microphones sensitive to frequencies far above the range of human hearing revealed that bats were emitting a constant stream of high-pitched calls.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle that the bats were using, now known as echolocation, is conceptually simple. The animal produces a sound and then listens for the echoes that return from objects in its surroundings. The delay between the call and the echo indicates how far away an object is, while differences between the echoes arriving at the left and right ears reveal its direction. By comparing successive echoes, a bat can calculate whether an insect is approaching or moving away, and even estimate its size and texture. The computational demands of this process are considerable, and the auditory regions of a bat's brain are correspondingly enlarged and highly specialised.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Bats do not all call in the same way, and the differences reflect where and how they hunt. Species that pursue insects in open air tend to emit long, low-frequency calls, which travel considerable distances before fading. Those that forage among dense vegetation, by contrast, use short calls that sweep rapidly across a wide band of frequencies. Such calls carry less far, but they provide extremely detailed information about nearby surfaces, allowing the bat to separate an insect from the leaves on which it rests. A small number of species also exploit the Doppler effect, detecting the minute changes in pitch produced by the beating wings of their prey. The design of a call therefore represents a compromise between range and resolution, and field recordings allow specialists to identify many species purely from the acoustic signatures they leave on a detector, a technique now routinely employed in ecological surveys.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: As a bat closes in on its target, its calling pattern changes dramatically. During the search phase, it may produce around ten calls per second. Once an insect has been detected, the rate increases, and in the final moments before capture it can exceed two hundred calls per second, a burst that researchers describe as the 'terminal buzz'. Producing sound at this rate requires some of the fastest muscles known in any mammal. At the same time, the bat must avoid being deafened by its own calls, which can be extremely loud; a special muscle in the middle ear contracts at the moment each call is produced, briefly reducing the bat's sensitivity.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Insects have not remained passive in the face of this threat. Many moths possess simple ears tuned to the frequencies of bat calls, and when they detect an approaching bat they perform sudden dives or erratic loops. Some species go further, producing clicks of their own. In certain cases these clicks appear to warn the bat that the moth is distasteful, while in others they seem to interfere with the bat's ability to process its echoes. Bats, in turn, have developed counter-strategies, including calls at frequencies that moths cannot easily hear, an example of the evolutionary contest between predator and prey.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, however, to assume that every bat relies on echolocation. Many large fruit bats navigate largely by sight and smell, and their eyes are well adapted to low light. A few fruit bat species do echolocate, but instead of producing sound in the larynx, they generate clicks with their tongues, a technique that is cruder but evidently adequate for finding their way into dark caves. Furthermore, even the most sophisticated echolocating bats use other senses. There is growing evidence that some species can detect the Earth's magnetic field, which may help them orient themselves during long-distance migration. Vision, too, appears more important than was once assumed: experiments indicate that many insect-eating species use their eyes to recognise landmarks at dusk, reserving echolocation for the precise manoeuvres that hunting demands.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Echolocation research has also inspired practical applications. Engineers developing navigation aids for visually impaired people have studied how bats extract information from echoes, and some devices now convert ultrasonic reflections into audible tones. Of perhaps greater significance is the finding that some blind people teach themselves to echolocate by making clicking sounds with their mouths. Brain scans of these individuals suggest that they process echoes in regions normally associated with vision, indicating a remarkable degree of flexibility in the human brain. Bats, it seems, are not the only mammals capable of seeing with sound.

texts.title: Insurance for the harvest? Seed banks and the future of crops

paragraphs.text: Deep inside a mountain on a remote Arctic archipelago lies a facility that has been described, with some journalistic licence, as a doomsday vault. Its purpose is to store duplicate samples of seeds held by genebanks around the world, so that if a national collection is lost through war, natural disaster or simple mismanagement, the material can be recovered. The vault has attracted enormous public attention, and it is easy to see why: the image of humanity's agricultural heritage sealed safely in the permafrost is undeniably reassuring. Yet the vault is only the most visible element of a far larger and less glamorous network, and the reassurance it offers deserves closer scrutiny.

The rationale for conserving crop diversity is compelling. Over roughly ten thousand years, farmers selected and exchanged seeds, producing an extraordinary variety of locally adapted forms of every major crop. These traditional varieties, often called landraces, contain genetic traits that may prove indispensable as climates change and new diseases emerge: tolerance of drought or salinity, resistance to particular pests, or the ability to mature in a shorter season. During the twentieth century, however, the spread of high-yielding modern varieties led farmers in many regions to abandon their landraces, and with them, potentially irreplaceable genetic resources. Genebanks were established largely in response to this loss. International research centres began systematic collecting expeditions, and national governments created their own repositories, so that today several million samples are held in more than a thousand institutions worldwide, although a considerable proportion of these are duplicates of one another.

The basic technology of seed conservation is surprisingly straightforward. Most seeds of temperate crops can be preserved for decades if they are dried to a low moisture content and then stored at temperatures well below freezing. Under these conditions, metabolic processes slow almost to a halt. Nevertheless, seeds do not survive indefinitely, and their viability must be tested at intervals. When germination rates fall below an acceptable threshold, the sample has to be regenerated: planted, grown to maturity and harvested again. This is the most demanding and expensive aspect of genebank management, and it is here that many collections, particularly in poorer countries, have struggled. Inadequate electricity supplies, shortages of trained personnel and unpredictable funding have all contributed to the deterioration of samples that were originally stored with considerable care.

Moreover, not all crops are amenable to this approach. The seeds of many tropical species, including cocoa and several important fruits, are described as recalcitrant: they are killed by drying and cannot be frozen. Other crops, such as potatoes, cassava and bananas, are usually propagated vegetatively rather than from seed, so they must be maintained as living plants in field collections or as tissue cultures in laboratories. Both alternatives are costly and vulnerable to disease, and research into freezing plant tissue in liquid nitrogen, though promising, has not yet been applied on a wide scale. For a significant proportion of the world's food plants, then, the image of seeds safely asleep in a vault is simply inaccurate.

A more fundamental criticism concerns the nature of what is being preserved. A genebank conserves a snapshot of diversity as it existed at the moment of collection. In the field, by contrast, landraces continue to evolve, exposed to shifting climates and changing populations of pests and pathogens. Advocates of on-farm conservation argue that this ongoing adaptation is itself a resource of great value, and that freezing samples, while necessary, cannot substitute for supporting the farmers who still cultivate traditional varieties. In my view, this argument is persuasive. The two strategies should be regarded as complementary, yet funding has historically favoured the more tangible achievement of building and stocking storage facilities.

There are also questions of access and ownership. Many of the samples in international collections were gathered from farmers in developing countries, who received little or nothing in return. Subsequent international agreements have attempted to ensure that the benefits arising from the use of these resources, for example in commercial plant breeding, are shared fairly. How effectively these arrangements work in practice is disputed, and some farming communities remain wary of handing over seeds that represent generations of their own selection. It would be naive to dismiss such concerns as obstacles to scientific progress; trust is a prerequisite for the cooperation on which conservation depends.

None of this is to suggest that seed banks are unimportant. On the contrary, there are documented cases in which material held in genebanks has been used to restore crops to regions where local varieties had been lost, including after armed conflicts. Wild relatives of crops stored in collections have supplied genes for disease resistance that have protected harvests worth considerable sums. The danger lies rather in treating storage as a complete solution, an insurance policy that allows us to neglect the living systems from which diversity originally emerged. A vault in the Arctic is an admirable precaution, but the future of crops will be decided at least as much in farmers' fields.

tasks.prompt: The maps below show the village of Elmbrook in 2000 and at the present time. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
key_features: Overview: Elmbrook has become more built-up and residential, with farmland and part of the woodland replaced, while the road, river and older houses are unchanged.
The farmland north of the main road has been replaced by a housing estate.
The woodland has been reduced to make room for a car park.
The shop has become a larger supermarket, and the primary school has been extended.
A footbridge now crosses the river south of the houses.

model_answer.text:
The maps illustrate how the village of Elmbrook has changed between 2000 and the present day.

Overall, the village has become considerably more developed and residential. Much of the open land to the north of the main road has been built on, and several existing facilities have been enlarged, whereas the road, the river and the original houses have remained in place.

In 2000, the area north of the main road consisted of farmland on the western side and woodland on the eastern side. Today, the farmland has been entirely replaced by a housing estate. The woodland has also shrunk to roughly half its former size, and part of the cleared land is now occupied by a car park.

South of the road, the small shop in the west has been converted into a supermarket, which covers a larger area. The block of houses in the centre of the village is unchanged, but the primary school to the east has been extended. Finally, a footbridge has been constructed across the river, giving residents direct access to the southern bank, which previously could not be reached from the village.

tasks.prompt: Some people believe that unpaid community service, such as helping in hospitals or cleaning public parks, should be a compulsory part of every teenager's education. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
key_features: A clear position (agree, disagree or partly agree) stated in the introduction and kept throughout.
Benefits of community service for teenagers and for society, with specific examples.
Possible problems of making it compulsory (pressure on study time, lack of genuine motivation, supervision costs).
A reasoned conclusion that follows from the arguments, possibly suggesting how such a scheme could work well.

model_answer.text:
In many countries, schools are under pressure to prepare young people not only for examinations but also for life as responsible citizens. One proposal is to make unpaid community work a required part of secondary education. In my view, this is a valuable idea, provided that it is organised flexibly and with genuine choice.

The strongest argument in favour is that community service exposes teenagers to people and problems they might otherwise never encounter. A sixteen-year-old who spends a few hours a week reading to elderly residents in a care home, for instance, is likely to develop patience and empathy that no classroom lesson can teach. Such experiences can also help young people discover interests that shape their future careers, whether in medicine, social work or environmental management. Furthermore, society benefits directly, since parks are cleaner and overstretched services receive practical help.

Critics argue that compulsion undermines the very spirit of volunteering. If students are forced to participate, they may do the minimum required and gain little from the experience. There is also a legitimate concern that teenagers already face heavy academic workloads, and that additional obligations could increase stress, especially for those who have part-time jobs or care for family members.

These objections, however, are arguments for careful design rather than for abandoning the idea. If schools allowed students to choose from a wide range of projects, limited the commitment to a manageable number of hours, and recognised the work in their final records, most of the difficulties could be avoided.

In conclusion, I largely agree that community service should be part of every teenager's education, as long as it is flexible and meaningful rather than a box-ticking exercise.
